title: Understanding English Grammar and Sentence Anatomy
orientation: Grammar helps you see how a message is built before you try to improve it. When you read instructions, explain an event or edit a paragraph, you need to know which words belong together and what role each group performs. Today introduces the tools for that work: meaningful parts inside words, grammatical word classes, phrases, clauses and the main elements of a sentence. You do not need to memorise every exception today. Learn the basic distinctions and practise explaining a few short sentences accurately. The later days develop each word class and construction in detail. Advanced panels introduce terminology you may meet in university grammars; you can return to them after the foundation practice. Treat reading, recognition and independent writing as separate activities: recognising a label does not yet show that you can construct or revise the corresponding pattern.
outcomes: Distinguish a word class from a grammatical function.
Segment a transparent word into a root and relevant affixes.
Identify a whole subject phrase, its head and a simple predicate.
Distinguish direct objects, predicative complements and adjuncts in taught examples.
Explain a meaning difference caused by changing subject and object.

modules.title: Grammar, meaning and units of structure
modules.definition: Grammar describes the patterns by which words and larger units combine and change form. A grammatical analysis asks how an expression is built; interpretation asks what it means in a particular context. Neither question can be answered reliably by word order alone.
foundation: Begin with a familiar message: The nurse opened the window. Its words work together to identify someone, an event and something affected. Reversing nurse and window changes who does what, even though most words remain unchanged. Grammar therefore carries meaning. Vocabulary also matters: The window congratulated the nurse follows a recognisable structural pattern but normally needs an imaginative context. Structural well-formedness and ordinary real-world plausibility are different judgements. When evaluating an unfamiliar sentence, identify which judgement you are making before calling it wrong.
intermediate: A phrase is a unit organised around a head, its central word; it can contain one word or several. In the unusually quiet room, room heads a noun phrase, quiet heads an adjective phrase and unusually is an adverb. A clause organises a situation around a verb, often with a subject and complements. The nurse opened the window is a finite clause. To open the window is a non-finite clause: its verb has no independent tense. This course introduces these terms now and analyses their internal structure in Days 13–15.
advanced: A full written sentence normally contains a main clause and appropriate boundary punctuation. A subordinate clause can be part of that sentence: The nurse opened the window because the room was warm. Because introduces a reason but does not make the first event happen in the grammar itself; the writer asserts that causal relationship. Short answers, labels and conversational fragments can be meaningful without a full main clause. No entry on a sign and After lunch in reply to When? are useful expressions; formal paragraph writing normally requires fuller structures.
expert: Grammatical correctness, contextual acceptability and editorial style must be distinguished. A sentence may be grammatical but too informal for a report, or perfectly clear in conversation but unclear without its shared setting. Standard British and American forms can differ without one being a mistake. A descriptive account records established patterns; a prescriptive convention recommends choices for a stated purpose. In this course, British English supplies the editorial default, while alternatives are identified explicitly. An asterisk in a grammar book often marks an unacceptable intended reading; it does not prove every imaginable use impossible.

patterns.meaning: The second clause supplies the writer’s reason for the first situation.

examples.analysis: A main clause forms a complete neutral written statement.

examples.sentence: The courier arrived after the office closed.
examples.analysis: A subordinate time clause locates the arrival relative to the closure.

examples.sentence: To reach the archive before noon, Sara took an earlier bus.
examples.analysis: The opening non-finite clause states a purpose; Sara is understood as the person reaching the archive.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical; exchanging subjects and objects changes the roles and meaning.

exceptions: Close the window is a grammatical imperative with an ordinarily unexpressed subject. Do not add you merely to satisfy a simplified statement that every sentence must display a subject.

mistakes.problem: Because the lift had stopped. We used the stairs.
mistakes.repair: Because the lift had stopped, we used the stairs.
mistakes.reason: For a continuous formal statement, attach the reason clause to its main clause.

mistakes.problem: The clerk opened the file the supervisor read it.
mistakes.repair: The clerk opened the file, and the supervisor read it.
mistakes.reason: Two main clauses need an appropriate boundary or grammatical link.

glossary.definition: A grammatical unit organised around a verb, with finite or non-finite structure.
glossary.example: The staff waited is finite; to wait outside is non-finite.

glossary.definition: The central element that determines a phrase’s category.
glossary.example: In the small office, office heads the noun phrase.

modules.title: Inside words: morphemes, roots, stems and word formation
modules.definition: A morpheme is a smallest unit carrying lexical meaning or grammatical information. A root supplies the central lexical material; a stem is the form to which an inflection is attached. Inflection supplies grammatical forms, while derivation creates a new lexical item.
foundation: Compare help, helpful and helpfulness. Help carries the central meaning; -ful helps form an adjective, and -ness helps form a noun. These added parts cannot normally stand alone as words, so they are bound morphemes. Help can stand alone, making it a free morpheme. Meaningful parts are not the same as syllables: helpfulness has three readily identifiable morphemes, but a long word need not contain a meaningful part for each syllable. Avoid splitting letters into pieces unless each piece has a defensible role in contemporary English.
intermediate: Inflection relates forms of one lexical item: file/files, walk/walked/walking and small/smaller. Derivation changes the vocabulary item: teach/teacher or happy/unhappy/happiness. Derivation can change word class, as happy to happiness does, but need not: happy and unhappy are both adjectives. In teachers, teach is the root, teacher is the stem receiving the plural ending and -s marks plural number. A base is the material to which an affix attaches at a particular step; it can already contain other affixes. These labels describe different analytical roles rather than competing spellings.
advanced: A prefix precedes its base, as un- in unfair; a suffix follows it, as -ment in agreement. Compounding combines lexical bases: raincoat or classroom. Conversion uses an established form in a new class without an overt affix: a text and to text. Spelling does not supply a perfect guide to structure: compounds may be closed, hyphenated or written separately. Learn a new word together with its meaning, word class and usual pattern. A productive pattern permits new formations readily, but a familiar suffix cannot be added freely to every possible base.
expert: Roots and stems can be irregular or show changes of spelling and sound. The past went is an inflectional form of go even though it is not built by visibly adding -ed. Morphological analysis is therefore more than chopping off endings. Contemporary structure also differs from etymology, the historical origin of a word: learners need not reconstruct ancient roots before understanding a current English form. This introductory model intentionally avoids deciding every disputed boundary, such as the status of English possessive -’s; that construction receives a phrase-level account on Day 2.

patterns.meaning: teach + -er + -s forms a plural noun meaning people who teach.

examples.analysis: garden + -er forms a person noun; plural -s gives gardeners.
un- derives unfair from fair without changing adjective class.
Email is used as a verb here; its form does not require a new derivational ending.

contrasts.note: Reviewed is an inflected verb form; reviewer is a derived noun. The shared ending letters are not interchangeable.

exceptions: Some grammatical contrasts have no visible added suffix: sheep may be singular or plural. Interpret the word with its determiner, verb and context.

mistakes.reason: Perfect auxiliary has requires a past participle; went is the past-simple form.
Inventing a suffix does not create a standard adjective; clear is the needed predicative form here.

glossary.definition: A grammatical form change within a lexical item.
glossary.example: Worked is a past form of work.

glossary.definition: Formation of a new lexical item, often by an affix.

modules.title: Word classes and the difference between category and function
modules.definition: A word class is a grammatical category identified through a combination of form, distribution and possible combinations. A function is a role within a larger structure. Noun is a category; subject and modifier are functions. A word’s meaning alone does not establish its class.
foundation: Nouns commonly head expressions naming people, things or ideas: teacher, bridge, patience. Verbs organise actions, events or states: repair, happen, know. Adjectives commonly describe or classify nouns: a narrow bridge. Adverbs modify activities, qualities, other adverbs or wider statements: works carefully, unusually narrow, fortunately. These are major open classes: new members enter them readily. Many words have more than one class, so classify their use in a particular sentence. The spelling clean occurs as an adjective in a clean room and as a verb in clean the room.
intermediate: Other classes include determiners, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections. Determiners help specify a noun’s reference or quantity: the report, this report, some reports. Pronouns can head expressions such as she, someone or mine. Prepositions head relational expressions: under the table, after lunch. Conjunctions link units: paper and ink; because it rained. Interjections express reactions: Oh! These are relatively closed classes, although change is possible. Closed does not mean semantically empty: compare before lunch with after lunch, where one small word changes the time relationship.
advanced: Use several clues together. Plural marking often identifies nouns; comparison often identifies gradable adjectives; auxiliary patterns identify verbs. Each clue has exceptions. News is singular, wooden normally lacks comparative wooden-er, and fast is an adverb in move fast despite lacking -ly. A noun can modify another noun: in a stone wall, stone remains a noun functioning as a premodifier. An adjective can follow a linking verb: the wall is old. Category and position therefore interact, but neither simply equals the other. Detailed patterns are developed in the dedicated noun, verb and adjective lessons.
expert: Grammars differ in some category boundaries. Traditional accounts often call my a possessive adjective; this course usually calls it a possessive determiner because it occupies a determiner position. Some modern accounts treat pronouns as a subclass of nouns or distinguish determinative as a word class from determiner as a function. Recognise the labels without assuming the analysis has changed the sentence’s meaning. The immediate goal is a defensible explanation supported by behaviour: name the category, then state its function in the expression. Do not turn every describing word into an adjective or every -ly word into an adverb.

patterns.meaning: The adjective modifies the noun; the determiner specifies reference.
The first noun can function as a modifier without changing class.

examples.sentence: Those careful researchers checked the figures.
examples.analysis: Those is a determiner, careful an adjective and researchers the noun head.

examples.sentence: The college will finance the project.
examples.analysis: Finance is a lexical verb after modal will; the project is its object.

examples.sentence: The finance office remained open unusually late.
examples.analysis: Finance is a noun modifier, open is an adjective complement, and unusually modifies adverb late.

contrasts.note: Friendly is an adjective despite -ly; quietly is an adverb. Endings are clues, not decisive rules.

exceptions: One spelling can belong to different classes: They water the plants uses a verb, while The water is cold uses a noun. Explain the local pattern rather than assign one permanent label to the spelling.

mistakes.problem: A stone wall: stone must be an adjective because it describes wall.
mistakes.repair: Stone is a noun functioning as a modifier of wall.
mistakes.reason: Category and modifying function must be distinguished.
In this intended manner description, the adverb calmly modifies answered; calm is the adjective form.

glossary.definition: A category such as noun, verb or adjective.
glossary.example: In They plan carefully, plan is a verb.

glossary.definition: A role such as subject, object or modifier.
glossary.example: The noun phrase those plans functions as subject in Those plans changed.

modules.title: Subjects, predicates and the first sentence patterns
modules.definition: The subject is a grammatical element identified by structural behaviour, not simply the person doing an action. The predicate is what is predicated of that subject. Objects, predicative complements and adjuncts perform different roles within clause structure.
foundation: Start with The librarian opened the parcel. The librarian is the subject; opened the parcel is the predicate. Opened is the verb and the parcel is the direct object. In a neutral declarative clause, English usually places these in subject–verb–object order, abbreviated SVO. Identify the whole subject phrase before naming its head: in The new librarian opened the parcel, the new librarian is the subject and librarian is its head. Keeping those two answers separate prevents a common analysis mistake. The predicate can be short or extended with additional information.
intermediate: Not every clause has an object. The visitors waited follows subject–verb, or SV. The room became quiet contains a linking verb and a subject complement: quiet describes the room rather than a separate affected object. A complement can be a noun phrase: Leena is a doctor. In The coach gave the players advice, the players is an indirect object and advice is the direct object. In They considered the advice useful, useful is an object complement, describing the advice. Learn these contrasts as meaningful patterns rather than force all sentences into SVO.
advanced: Adjuncts add circumstances or comments: The visitors waited outside yesterday. Outside gives place and yesterday gives time. A complement is selected by a head’s pattern; an adjunct supplies a less tightly selected addition. With put, a location normally completes the pattern: Put the parcel on the desk. Deletion is a helpful clue, not an infallible test, since some selected complements can be left understood. A passive subject can be affected rather than an agent: The parcel was opened by the librarian. Subject is therefore a syntactic function, while agent and patient describe semantic roles.
expert: The course uses verb narrowly for the verbal element and predicate broadly for everything predicated of the subject. In broader syntactic terminology, objects are also complements because the verb selects them; when distinguishing clause patterns, subject complement and object complement mean predicative descriptions. State which sense of complement is intended. Dummy it in It is raining and dummy there in There are two seats occupy subject positions without naming an ordinary participant. Questions and some emphatic clauses change ordinary word order, so the first noun before a verb is not a universal subject test. These constructions receive detailed treatment later.

patterns.meaning: A transitive clause: The mechanic repaired the bicycle.
A predicative clause: The bicycle looks new.

examples.analysis: SV: the musicians is subject; rehearsed is the verb and complete predicate.

examples.sentence: The volunteers painted the classroom yesterday.
examples.analysis: SVO plus time adjunct: yesterday is outside the object noun phrase.

examples.sentence: The board considered the proposed timetable impractical.
examples.analysis: The proposed timetable is direct object; impractical is its predicative complement.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. Became takes a subject complement; appointed takes an object in this use.

exceptions: Imperatives normally omit an expressed subject: Read the notice. Questions can put an auxiliary before the subject: Did the visitors wait? Analyse the whole pattern.

mistakes.problem: The head of the two departments approve the plan.
mistakes.repair: The head of the two departments approves the plan.
mistakes.reason: The head of the two departments is the subject; singular head controls ordinary agreement here.
The intended description of the room is the adjective quiet, functioning as subject complement.

glossary.definition: An element normally selected by a transitive verb, typically a noun phrase.
An added circumstance or comment rather than a selected complement.
glossary.example: Yesterday is a time adjunct in We met yesterday.

questions.prompt: In The gardener watered the roses, which expression is the whole subject?
questions.why: The complete noun phrase The gardener is the subject; gardener alone is its head, watered is the verb, and the roses is the object.

questions.prompt: In the transparent analysis teach + -er + -s, which part marks plural number?
questions.why: Plural -s is inflectional. Teach is the root, -er forms the person noun, and teacher is the stem receiving the plural ending.

questions.prompt: In They will chair the discussion, what is the class of chair?
questions.why: Chair follows modal will as a plain-form lexical verb and selects the discussion as its object.

questions.prompt: In The parcel was opened by Amina, which statement about the parcel is accurate?
options: It is the agent because every subject is an agent.
It is an adjunct because the clause is passive.
It is the subject and is affected by the opening.
It is the direct object because it is affected.
questions.why: Passive subjects can denote affected participants. Subject is a grammatical function; agent is a semantic role.

questions.prompt: Which expression is a non-finite clause in the analysis used here?
questions.why: To repair contains a non-finite verbal head and its object. The other choices are noun or prepositional phrases.

questions.prompt: In a school library, what is the usual analysis of school?
options: a noun functioning as a modifier
an adjective because all modifiers are adjectives
questions.why: A noun may modify another noun without becoming an adjective. School and library are both nouns here.

questions.prompt: Check the three labelled parts in neutral formal prose: The new assistant [A] / seems [B] / patiently [C]. Choose the faulty part or No error.
questions.why: The intended property of the assistant requires patient, a predicative adjective. The subject and linking verb are well formed.

questions.prompt: Check the labels: The visitors [A] / waited [B] / outside [C]. Choose the faulty part or No error.
questions.why: Waited is intransitive here and outside supplies place. No object is required.

questions.prompt: Which pair illustrates derivation rather than merely two inflections of one lexical item?
questions.why: Kindness is a new noun formed from an adjective; the other pairs supply grammatical forms within the same lexical item.

questions.prompt: In The explanation made the audience uneasy, what is uneasy?
questions.why: Uneasy predicates a property of the audience, the direct object of made. It does not name another recipient or participant.

questions.prompt: Arrange these units as a neutral statement: the gate / opened / the guard.
rubric: Place the guard as subject before opened.
Keep the gate as object; preserve the opening event.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Bracket the whole subject and object: Three tired passengers missed the final bus.
questions.model: [Three tired passengers] subject; [the final bus] direct object.
rubric: Include the modifiers within each noun phrase.
Distinguish each full phrase from its head.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Classify clean in a clean desk and Please clean the desk.
questions.model: Adjective in a clean desk; verb in Please clean the desk.
rubric: Use the local pattern as evidence.
Do not assign one class to both occurrences.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Segment helpers into meaningful parts and name the role of each.
questions.model: help + -er + -s: lexical root, person-forming derivational suffix, plural inflection.
rubric: Identify all three meaningful units.
Distinguish derivation from plural marking.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Compare Rida became a manager with Rida hired a manager.
questions.model: A manager describes Rida after became, so it is a subject complement; it names a separately hired participant after hired, so it is an object.
rubric: Identify the two functions.
Explain the relation to Rida rather than rely only on position.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Join The door was locked and The caretaker used a spare key using because; state that the lock explains the key use.
questions.model: The caretaker used a spare key because the door was locked.
rubric: Retain both situations.
Make the locked door the reason, not the result.
alternatives: Because the door was locked, the caretaker used a spare key.

questions.prompt: Split into two full statements without losing either event: The lecturer arrived, and the students opened their notebooks.
questions.model: The lecturer arrived. The students opened their notebooks.
rubric: Give each event a main clause.
Use appropriate written sentence boundaries.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Identify the determiner, adjective and noun head in those difficult questions.
questions.model: Those: determiner; difficult: adjective; questions: noun head.
rubric: Account for all three words.
Separate their categories from the phrase’s possible clause function.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Identify the adjunct in The laboratory closed early and say what it contributes.
questions.model: Early is a time adjunct indicating an earlier closing than a contextual expectation.
rubric: Identify early.
Explain its time meaning without calling it an object.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain why unhappy and happier illustrate different word-forming processes.
questions.model: Unhappy is derived from happy with negative un-; happier is the comparative inflection of happy.
rubric: Name derivation and inflection correctly.
Explain the meaning contributed by each form.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: A notice reads No parking. Explain why this need not be treated as a failed formal paragraph sentence.
questions.model: It is a conventional sign expressing a prohibition in abbreviated form; its function and context license a short expression.
rubric: Identify the sign context.
Distinguish meaningful minor expression from a full clause.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Supply a predicative adjective: After the long journey, the children felt ____. Explain its function.
questions.model: After the long journey, the children felt tired. Tired describes the children as subject complement.
rubric: Use an adjective compatible with the intended state.
Explain which participant it describes.
alternatives: Happy, hungry or another suitable adjective is acceptable.

questions.prompt: In Only the supervisor signed, explain why being beside a noun does not make only an adjective.
questions.model: Only focuses the noun phrase the supervisor; its restrictive meaning and distribution support an adverb analysis, despite its position near a noun.
rubric: Identify the focused phrase.
Avoid using adjacency as the sole classification test.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Analyse the predicate in The council gave the residents an explanation.
questions.model: Gave the residents an explanation is the predicate; gave is the verb, the residents the indirect object and an explanation the direct object.
rubric: Identify the full predicate.
Distinguish recipient from thing given.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Compare The dog followed the child and The child followed the dog. Are both grammatical, and what changes?
questions.model: Both are grammatical SVO clauses. The follower and followed participant exchange roles.
rubric: Recognise both as grammatical.
Describe the changed roles precisely.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain why went can be an inflection of go even though its letters do not contain go.
questions.model: An inflection belongs to a grammatical paradigm; it need not be formed by a visible added suffix. Went supplies the past-simple form of go.
rubric: Identify the past-simple relationship.
Reject visible suffixation as a necessary condition.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Repair the boundary and agreement faults: The manager of the two shops arrive early she opens the safe.
questions.model: The manager of the two shops arrives early. She opens the safe.
rubric: Use singular arrives with manager.
Separate the two main clauses appropriately.
alternatives: The manager of the two shops arrives early, and she opens the safe.

questions.prompt: Why does The timetable swallowed the clerk need context before its oddness can be classified?
questions.model: Its SVO structure is recognisable, but its literal meaning is unusual. A metaphorical context could license the idea of a timetable consuming the clerk’s attention.
rubric: Separate structural pattern from semantic plausibility.
Give a coherent possible metaphor without claiming the literal event is ordinary.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct for ordinary formal prose: The keeper of the records open the cupboard.
corrections.model: The keeper of the records opens the cupboard.
rubric: Identify keeper as the singular head.
Change open to opens without changing the subject.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

rubric: Use a predicative adjective.
Retain the meaning that the corridor became noisy.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct: We have wrote three messages.
rubric: Use the past participle after have.
Retain plural subject we and the object.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Repair the boundary in The screen went dark the technician restarted the machine.
corrections.model: The screen went dark, and the technician restarted the machine.
rubric: Keep both events.
Use a full stop, semicolon or suitable coordination.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: For a complete formal statement, repair Because the bridge was closed. The driver turned back.
corrections.model: Because the bridge was closed, the driver turned back.
rubric: Attach the subordinate reason clause.
Keep the causal relationship.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct the manner expression: The guide explained the route clear.
corrections.model: The guide explained the route clearly.
rubric: Use clearly for the intended manner of explaining.
Do not change route into an adjective.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if necessary: Close the side door.
rubric: Recognise a grammatical imperative.
Do not add an obligatory expressed subject.
alternatives: You close the side door changes emphasis; it is not a required repair.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if necessary: The new assistant is in the storeroom.
rubric: Recognise in the storeroom as a permitted predicative location.
Do not require every complement of be to be an adjective.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

transformations.prompt: Replace the object with an object pronoun: The nurse checked the instruments.
rubric: Use an object pronoun referring to plural instruments.
Keep subject, verb and event unchanged.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

transformations.prompt: Start with Because and preserve the reason: The corridor was crowded, so the staff used another entrance.
transformations.model: Because the corridor was crowded, the staff used another entrance.
rubric: Make crowding the reason.
Retain both clauses and appropriate punctuation.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

writing.prompt: Write a 60–90-word account of a routine at work, home or college. Include an SV clause, an SVO clause and a clause with a subject complement. Below the account, bracket one full subject and identify one adjunct.
writing.model:
The library opens early. A caretaker checks the windows before the first students arrive. The reading room is quiet, and the lamps are already on. Visitors leave their bags by the entrance. During the morning, the librarian answers questions and records new loans. A small reading group meets upstairs. Its members share books and discuss their different interpretations.

Analysis: The library opens early contains subject + verb with a time adjunct. A caretaker checks the windows contains subject, verb and direct object. The reading room is quiet contains subject, linking verb and subject complement. The reading room is a whole subject; room is its head.
rubric: Identify at least one valid SV, SVO and subject-complement pattern.
Give a complete subject phrase and a genuine adjunct.
Check sentence boundaries and preserve a coherent routine; alternative content is welcome.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Diagnostic recall: label paper in The paper tore and Please paper the wall.
recall.model: Noun in the first clause; verb in the second.
rubric: Use local distribution.
Treat conversion as possible.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Diagnostic recall: in The young engineer repaired the pump, identify the subject head and the whole subject.
recall.model: Head: engineer. Whole subject: The young engineer.
rubric: Distinguish head and phrase.
Include determiner and modifier in the whole subject.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Diagnostic recall: explain the structural difference between The meeting ended and after the meeting ended.
recall.model: The first is a main clause; adding after gives a subordinate time clause that normally joins a main clause in full formal prose.
rubric: Identify both as clauses.
Explain the effect of after.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

checklist: I can give both a category and a function for a word or phrase.
I distinguish a whole subject phrase from its head.
I can recognise a non-finite clause without pretending it carries its own tense.
I can explain why two grammatical sentences may mean different things.
I use structural evidence before declaring an unfamiliar expression wrong.
